reviewBoundary: Three complete junior reading practices: four full four-question passages, plus a four-email five-question thread and independent five-question reading. Fictional cases; same-author all-option/evidence/time-update review, no independent calibration.

units.title: A shop dog and a class photograph
units.alignmentNote: Two complete written four-question passages for junior2 explicitly adapt the written-reading part of its source. Junior3 retains a four-email thread with five questions plus a separate five-question reading, all three-choice. No source prose copied.

materials.title: Patch knows the closing time
materials.text:
The bicycle shop near our home has a dog called Patch. Every evening, just before closing, he brings his lead to Mr Lane at the counter. Customers often say the dog can tell the time better than they can.

I believed it until one Saturday when the shop closed early. Mr Lane had a family party and put a notice on the door saying he would leave at two. At a quarter to two, Patch was still asleep under a chair. I watched the clock, waiting for him to fetch the lead.

At five to two, Mr Lane switched off the radio and began putting the display bicycles inside. Patch opened his eyes. When the last bicycle crossed the doorway, the dog walked to his basket, picked up the lead and brought it to the counter.

I asked Mr Lane whether Patch had finally noticed the clock. He laughed and said the dog usually responded to the end-of-day routine. The quiet radio, moving bicycles and closing display were much more familiar signals than the hands on the wall.

The next week, I stayed until the normal closing time. Patch did not move when the clock reached the hour. He moved when Mr Lane finished the familiar jobs. I still liked the customers' story about a time-telling dog, but now I had another explanation to compare with it. Patch, meanwhile, seemed interested only in getting to the park.

questions.prompt: What do customers often say about Patch?
options: He knows when the shop should close
He repairs every bicycle himself
He chooses the radio programmes
He dislikes going for walks
questions.explanation: Fetching the lead near closing prompts the time-telling claim. Repair/radio choices are not stated and he wants a walk.

questions.prompt: Why does the shop close early one Saturday?
options: Patch has hidden all the bicycles
The clock has stopped
The park is permanently closed
Mr Lane has a family party
questions.explanation: The owner’s family party is the stated reason. Dog sabotage/clock failure/park closure are invented.

questions.prompt: What happens just before Patch fetches the lead?
options: The narrator changes the clock
The radio becomes louder
Mr Lane completes the familiar closing jobs
A customer buys a watch
questions.explanation: Radio off and display bikes inside precede fetching. No clock/watch change occurs, and the radio goes quiet.

questions.prompt: What does the narrator conclude from the later visit?
options: Patch may respond to the routine rather than the clock alone
Patch has learned every number on the wall
The first customer’s story is scientifically proven
Dogs can never notice human actions
questions.explanation: The repeated sequence supports routine cues. Number-reading/scientific proof/general inability are not established.

materials.title: The hat behind the class
materials.text:
Our class photograph was scheduled for the last lesson on Friday. We arrived with clean uniforms and stood where the photographer asked. At the back, our teacher Mrs James wore a bright paper hat that one of the younger classes had made for her.

The photographer took a formal picture first. He asked us to look towards the camera and keep our hands still. I could hear a few people trying not to laugh at the hat, but Mrs James stood perfectly seriously.

Then he said we could have a second, less formal picture. Mrs James took the hat off and placed it on the empty chair beside her. Everyone turned to see who would wear it next. At that exact moment, the camera clicked.

The second image showed thirty faces looking in different directions. Mine was turned almost completely away. I thought it would be deleted, but Mrs James asked for a copy along with the formal one.

A week later, both photographs appeared on the classroom wall. The first showed our faces clearly; the second reminded us of the moment before we began laughing. Mrs James wrote the date under each, without calling either the only proper record of the class.

When my parents saw them, they found me more quickly in the formal picture. In the other, they recognised my habit of turning towards whatever was happening. The photographs did different jobs, and I was glad that the photographer had not stopped after the first click.

questions.prompt: Why is the teacher’s hat unusual?
options: It belongs to the photographer’s horse
It is a bright paper hat made by younger pupils
It is part of every student’s uniform
It hides the whole camera
questions.explanation: The opening explains the handmade bright hat. Uniform/camera obstruction/horse ownership are not stated.

questions.prompt: What is the first photograph intended to show?
options: The paper hat without any people
Everyone looking away at once
Only an empty chair
Clear formal faces looking towards the camera
questions.explanation: The photographer requests camera-facing stillness. The other choices describe neither that request nor its result.

questions.prompt: Why do students turn in the second picture?
options: They are told the building is closing
The camera has disappeared
Their parents call from the door
They wonder who will wear the hat next
questions.explanation: The hat goes onto an empty chair and attracts attention. Alarm/parents/disappearing equipment are absent.

questions.prompt: Why are both pictures kept?
options: They show different aspects of the class and the event
The first has no students in it
The second is the only one with recognisable faces
The photographer is unable to take any formal image
questions.explanation: One clear record and one moment/habit record serve different purposes. The alternatives contradict the first picture’s success.

units.title: A letter team and a postcard stand
units.alignmentNote: Two complete written four-question passages for junior2 explicitly adapt the written-reading part of its source. Junior3 retains a four-email thread with five questions plus a separate five-question reading, all three-choice. No source prose copied.

materials.title: Four letters on four shirts
materials.text:
For an English activity, four students wore large letter cards on their shirts: S, E, A and T. Their first task was to stand in a line to make a word for something we sit on. They quickly formed SEAT, and the class clapped.

Our teacher then asked them to keep the same letters but show a direction. They looked puzzled until one student moved to the front. After a little rearranging, the line read EAST. Nobody had needed a new card.

The next challenge was to form a word about eating. The students changed places again and made EATS. A classmate asked whether they could make every English word by moving the four cards around. The teacher wrote BOOK on the board. We could not make it because the needed letters were not available.

We recorded the successful arrangements and their meanings. The activity was not just about moving quickly. A line could use all four letters and still fail to make the word the clue required. We had to check both the spelling and the meaning.

At the end, the four students mixed their cards on a table. We put them in an envelope labelled with the exact letters, not simply "English game". Another class could then choose suitable clues before using the set. The letters were a small resource; knowing what they could and could not do made the game easier to prepare.

questions.prompt: What word is formed first?
options: EAST
BOOK
SEAT
EATS
questions.explanation: The sitting clue produces SEAT first. EAST/EATS are later, BOOK impossible with these cards.

questions.prompt: What remains unchanged between SEAT and EAST?
options: Every student’s position
The order of the letters
The available four letters
The meaning of the word
questions.explanation: Cards stay S/E/A/T while positions, order and meaning change.

questions.prompt: Why can the group not form BOOK?
options: BOOK is not an English word
They have already used all English words
Every card is blank
They lack the required letters
questions.explanation: The available set lacks B/O/K. The alternatives are false or unsupported.

questions.prompt: Why does the envelope name the exact letters?
options: To help another class select possible clues
To prevent anyone learning spelling
To guarantee every possible word can be formed
To show the students’ shirt sizes
questions.explanation: Resource details support suitable clue planning. Universality/prevention/shirt size are not the label’s purpose.

materials.title: The postcard stand outside the library
materials.text:
A small stand outside our library offered postcards showing local buildings. Visitors could take one and leave a short note about the place on the back of another. The library staff planned to display a selection of the notes at the town festival.

I chose a card showing the old swimming baths. My first message described how they looked from the road. Then I saw a note from a man who had learned to swim there fifty years earlier. He remembered the cold changing room and the sound of children calling across the water.

The two notes were about the same building, but one described a present-day view and the other a past experience. I added a date and made clear that I had never been inside. I did not need to borrow the man's memory to make my note worth keeping.

A staff member checked that contributors understood which notes might be publicly displayed. People could choose not to add their names, and private contact details were not part of the display. The project collected stories, not a public list of everyone's address.

At the festival, my note appeared beside several very different ones. A drawing by a child showed the building as a giant blue fish. It was labelled as an imagined design. I liked the mixture because the labels allowed us to enjoy memory, observation and imagination without having to pretend they were the same kind of account.

questions.prompt: What does the postcard project invite visitors to contribute?
options: A complete address list for public display
A short note about a local place
Only professionally written histories
Their private passwords
questions.explanation: Short local-place notes are invited. Passwords/contact lists/professional-only rules are not part of it.

questions.prompt: How does the older man’s note differ from the narrator’s first note?
options: It claims the narrator learned swimming there
It contains only a current road view
It describes a future building on another planet
It recalls using the building in the past
questions.explanation: The man recalls lessons fifty years earlier. The narrator’s own view is external/current.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator say they have never been inside?
options: To prevent any other note being shown
To make the basis of the note clear
To prove the building never had an interior
To copy the man’s experience exactly
questions.explanation: The statement identifies an observed outside view rather than borrowed memory. The other claims are not intended.

questions.prompt: Why can the blue-fish drawing be included without confusion?
options: Everyone is told it is a historical photograph
All other labels have been removed
It is labelled as an imagined design
It proves the baths were a real fish
questions.explanation: Explicit imaginative status separates it from observation/history. The alternatives erase or falsify that label.

units.title: A model-boat workshop and a visitor’s question

materials.title: Four workshop messages
materials.text:
From: Mr Cole
Sent: Monday, 09:10
To: Workshop helpers
Subject: Saturday model boats
Our model-boat workshop will run from 10:00 to 12:00 in the art room on Saturday. Please arrive at 9:20 to arrange materials. Twelve students are booked. We provide card, glue and the other equipment, but each participant should bring a box for carrying the model home. Helpers need their badges.

From: Priya
Sent: Tuesday, 17:30
To: Mr Cole and helpers
Subject: Re: Saturday model boats
I can help prepare the room, but I have to leave at 11:30. Will that cause a problem for clearing up? I can still bring the display boat we made last term. It is already in a protective box, so I do not need anyone else to pack it.

From: Mr Cole
Sent: Wednesday, 12:15
To: Workshop helpers
Subject: Extra places and room change
We have accepted four more students, making sixteen altogether. The art room is being used for another event, so our workshop will be in Room 5. Times are unchanged. Lucas can stay to clear up, so Priya may leave as planned. Please use the new room number and total when making signs and setting out places.

From: Lucas
Sent: Friday, 16:00
To: Workshop helpers
Subject: Final reminder
I have put sixteen sets of materials in Room 5. The main gate opens at 9:30, so helpers arriving at 9:20 should use the side gate beside the library. A teacher will meet us there. Participants arriving for 10:00 can use the main gate. Badges are still required. Please do not bring extra glue; the school has supplied the approved materials.

questions.prompt: How many participants are expected?
options: Four
Twelve
Sixteen
questions.explanation: Wednesday adds4 to12 for16, confirmed Friday. Twelve is old total and four the increase.

questions.prompt: Where will the workshop take place?
options: Room 5
The art room
The library entrance
questions.explanation: Wednesday changes venue to Room5. The library marks helper entrance location.

questions.prompt: When may Priya leave?
options: Before 9:20
Only after 12:30
At 11:30 as planned
questions.explanation: Lucas covers cleanup, allowing the11:30 departure. Other times are not agreed.

questions.prompt: Which entrance should helpers use at 9:20?
options: The side gate beside the library
The main gate that opens at 9:30
The art-room window
questions.explanation: Friday explicitly directs early helpers to side gate. Main gate is not yet open, window not entry.

questions.prompt: What must a participant bring?
options: Extra school glue
A box to take the model home
A helper badge for every family member
questions.explanation: Monday requests a carrying box. Extra glue is prohibited and badges are for helpers.

materials.title: The question before the tour
materials.text:
Before our student guides led visitors around the school, we practised an introduction in the empty hall. I had memorised the date the building opened, the names of several past head teachers and a description of its architecture. I was proud that I could speak without looking at my notes.

The first visitor arrived carrying a small child. Before I could begin, she asked where she could leave a pushchair. I knew almost everything in my introduction except that. A member of staff showed her the suitable place, and I waited while she settled the child.

Our teacher later asked us to list the questions visitors had actually asked. Toilets, seats, lifts and the end time appeared more often than historical dates. This did not make the history unimportant. It showed what people needed to know before they could comfortably listen to it.

We revised the opening. A brief practical explanation came first, followed by the story of the hall. Staff checked the access information so that we would not promise a route or facility that was unavailable. We also agreed to ask for help when unsure rather than fill a gap with a guess.

On the next tour, a visitor asked an unexpected question about the old stage. I said I did not know and offered to pass it to the history teacher. The tour continued without disaster. I had become a more useful guide by learning which answers to prepare and which questions to take elsewhere, not by memorising a speech that could never be interrupted.

questions.prompt: What is the narrator initially proud of?
options: Providing all transport to the school
Speaking a memorised introduction without notes
Designing the whole building
Knowing every practical need of every visitor
questions.explanation: The narrator has memorised history/architecture and can speak without notes. Universal needs/design/transport are not claimed.

questions.prompt: What does the first visitor ask?
options: Whether she can be head teacher
Who designed every past building
For a copy of all school records
Where to leave a pushchair
questions.explanation: The immediate pushchair question interrupts the prepared historical opening.

questions.prompt: Why is practical information moved to the beginning?
options: The hall no longer exists
It helps visitors settle before listening to history
The school’s history has become forbidden
Every visitor already knows all the dates
questions.explanation: Visitor needs enable attention, without declaring history unimportant or universally known.

questions.prompt: Why do staff check the access information?
options: To stop all visitors using seats
To remove every practical detail
To avoid promising unavailable routes or facilities
To make every guide invent an answer
questions.explanation: The text explicitly checks availability before promises. Invention/removal/seat prohibition contradict the process.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator handle the stage question?
options: Pretends the visitor said nothing
Invents a date immediately
Admits not knowing and offers to ask the history teacher
Ends the tour in anger
questions.explanation: The final paragraph describes honest referral. Invention/anger/ignoring are not the response.
